How a Future Mars Lander Could 'Crush It' on the Surface

Something I always found ironic is that in trying to create 'guaranteed' landing systems various space administrations constantly create these sort of veritable rube goldberg landing systems. The latest failed lander, Schiaparelli from the ESA, was supposed to:

  • enter atmosphere
  • brake using heatshield and Mars' atmosphere while going 21,000 km/h
  • deploy parachute at 1650 km/h
  • release primary heatshield then start using a radar altimeter
  • jettison secondary heatshield and activate rocket propulsion at 1.3km above the surface
  • just before it hits the ground switch off the engines and then free fall to the ground landing on a crumple zone

There's just so many single points of failure there. And not to mention that these sort of strategies strictly limit the mass that can be landed. Atmospheric braking, parachutes, and crumple landings all just simply don't work as the masses involved increase. This is why I think what SpaceX is doing is so important. They're going to aim to land on Mars the same way they land they land their rockets back on Earth - using the thrusters to slow down the rocket and then landing on landing gear.

The problem of course is that the first rocket SpaceX does try this way of landing with stands a relatively good chance of becoming just another crater in Mars, assuming thrusting at supersonic atmospheric velocities doesn't result in it vaporizing before it even gets to the ground. But it's a process that once learned and perfected we can start landing arbitrarily large payloads on Mars with. But the risk aversion of government space industries means they can't afford to attempt landings unless they think a successful landing is extremely highly likely which of course paradoxically is playing a big role in why they keep failing.
